A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SpecPrune-VLA. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original LIBERO success rates, latency measurements, pruning experiments, component ablations, and evaluations on A800 and RTX 3090 GPUs.

after.justification: v2 reports original LIBERO experiments and adds π0 evaluation, LIBERO-plus robustness tests, physical-robot results, and further analyses in the appendices.

M1.justification: The two-level framework remains, but v1's mean/standard-deviation layer confidence is replaced by inverse attention entropy computed at the first inference and reused thereafter (v2 Equations 7–8). The velocity-based frame-selection rule also changes, and pruning layers shift from {5,10,15,20} to {10,15,20,25}. These alter the pruning procedure.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained four LIBERO suites, v2 evaluates 200 LIBERO-plus tasks with camera, lighting, background, and noise perturbations, and four physical manipulation tasks using a Flexiv Rizon4 arm. Appendix A.1.4 also adds action-mode analysis with UniVLA in SimplerEnv using a WidowX arm.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds FastV and DivPrune to the existing OpenVLA-OFT comparison while retaining SparseVLM, VLA-Cache, and EfficientVLA. It also introduces a separate comparison between unpruned π0 and π0 with SpecPrune-VLA, substantially broadening the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: The reported LIBERO configuration changes from suite-specific pruning ratios to a shared α=0.8. The early-layer overlap experiment changes from top-20 to top-30 tokens. New protocols include a controlled global-attention ablation with compensating local-token budgets, π0 evaluation, and real-robot fine-tuning and testing.

E4.justification: v2 extends the original component and pruning-ratio studies with explicit global-attention reuse and entropy-weighting ablations, layer-combination analysis, token-budget and velocity-threshold sensitivity, LIBERO-plus robustness tests, and cross-platform action-mode analysis. Tables 5–6 repeat Tables 2–3 and are not additional experiments.

E5.justification: v1 reports 40–50 repetitions per task and point-estimate benchmark tables. v2 newly reports multi-seed success-rate means ± half-range in Table 12 and ± module latencies in Table 9. It does not specify the seed/run count or retain the earlier repetition count, so an increase in repetitions cannot be established.

E6.justification: Reported LIBERO results change under the revised pruning configuration: Table 1's Spatial success rate changes from 98.2% to 97.4%. EfficientVLA's reported average speedup changes from 1.55× to 1.52×. v2 adds extensive ablation, robustness, π0, and physical-robot results, including 1.31× and 1.70× speedups for the latter two settings. These do not establish same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 revises the FLOP expression, changes M from attention-head count to FFN intermediate width, and replaces the rough reduction estimate with an explicit progressive-pruning cost sum and overhead complexity analysis. The Fourier-based viewpoint argument remains; neither version provides theorem or proof results.

C1.justification: The training-free, two-level pruning contribution remains, but the headline scope expands beyond OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO and two GPUs. v2's introduction claims effectiveness on π0, while its abstract and conclusion add 1.70× real-world acceleration and strong real-world generalization.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations distinguishing semantic middle-layer information from action-centric deep-layer information, motivates confidence through low attention entropy, and argues that normalized velocities support action recognition across robots and models. It adds hyperparameter failure explanations and removes v1's simulation-only limitation following physical-robot evaluation.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands reproducibility information with token budgets, velocity and similarity thresholds, raw-patch processing details, and module overhead measurements. Appendix A.5.5 and Table 13 document demonstration counts, preprocessing, LoRA rank 32, 80–100K training steps, eight H200 training GPUs, and RTX 4090 evaluation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and discussion for FastV, DivPrune, attention-entropy weighting, and SpeContext, together with sources supporting the new evaluations. References such as AdaSkip and Qwen2-VL disappear. The central positioning around combining global history with local pruning information remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method explanations undergo extensive rewriting and condensation. Parameter selection and design-space exploration precede the main performance evaluation in v2; Algorithm 1 moves to the appendix, whose material is substantially reorganized. The separate limitations section is removed.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the overview and insight figures, converts v1's component-ablation table into Figure 8, separates success-rate and latency reporting across Tables 1 and 10, and adds robustness and robot visualizations. Appendix Figure 15 retains v1 Figure 11; v2 Figure 13 and Tables 5–6 duplicate main-text displays.

improvement.justification: Physical-robot experiments directly address v1's explicitly stated simulation-only limitation. Targeted mechanism ablations, π0 evaluation, perturbation tests, and detailed implementation information substantially strengthen validation and reproducibility. Reporting weaknesses remain: run counts are unspecified, Tables 1 and 11 disagree on Spatial success, and the real-world conclusion overstates unchanged success despite two declines in Table 4. These temper but do not outweigh the gains.
